To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have identified QTLs for seedling lateral root length and lateral root number in maize, and that the QTLs can explain up to 40% of the phenotypic variation.
the genetic control of lateral root growth is complex and the genetic control of the plasticity of lateral root growth in response to phosphorus availability is not detected.

the genetic architecture of maize seedling root traits under varying phosphorus supply is highly complex and involves many QTLs with relatively small effects, and that the genetic variation for lateral root traits under varying P availability is sufficient to enable improvement of these traits by selection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the genetic basis for the plasticity of seedling lateral root length and number of maize under low and high phosphorous availability.
the development of maize germplasm with enhanced root growth under phosphorus stress.
the identification of QTLs that control lateral root development in maize seedlings and their plasticity in response to phosphorus supply.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

QTL mapping for lateral root length, lateral root number and plasticity in maize under differential phosphorus conditions is feasible, but that further studies are needed to validate and fine map the identified QTLs.
the genetic architecture of lateral root development under phosphorus deficiency is more complex than under phosphorus sufficiency.
the QTLs detected here for lateral root traits are associated with phosphorus uptake efficiency.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified QTLs that control lateral root growth and plasticity in maize under low phosphorus availability.
we have identified several chromosomal locations that contain genes controlling lateral root growth in response to phosphorus supply.
QTLs for LRL and LRL plasticity under low and high fertility were identified and that the QTLs for LRN and LRN plasticity under low fertility were identified.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there are genetic differences in the ability of maize genotypes to increase root length and number under phosphorus limitation, and that the genetic basis of this difference can be mapped to specific regions of the maize genome.
lateral root growth is an important trait in the adaptation of plants to low phosphorus environments.
there is a large amount of genetic variation in maize for root growth in response to P deficiency, and that it is possible to combine favorable alleles for this trait.
